prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A woman accused of killing her 2-year-old daughter and dumping her body in Galveston Bay in Texas has pleaded guilty to tampering with evidence in the case. Kimberly Dawn Trenor is scheduled to go on trial for murder next week in the death of her daughter. But Kimberly Dawn Trenor, 20, pleaded not guilty to the capital murder charge, her lawyer said Wednesday. Trenor and her husband, Royce Clyde Zeigler II, 25, both were charged with tampering with evidence and capital murder in the case of Riley Ann Sawyer, whose body was found in a large blue plastic container on an uninhabited island in Galveston Bay, Texas, in October 2007. The charge of tampering with evidence accused the couple of concealing the child's remains. Trenor was arraigned Tuesday in Galveston, Texas, said her lawyer, Tom Stickler. Jury selection for her trial on the capital murder charge begins Wednesday. The trial will begin in earnest on January 27, he said. The jury also will sentence Trenor on the evidence tampering charge, which carries a penalty of two to 20 years in prison, The Houston Chronicle reported. Zeigler, who is being tried separately, has not been formally arraigned, Stickler said. Both remain in jail. The Houston Chronicle reported bail had been set at $850,000 each. Riley Ann's case garnered national headlines after a fisherman found her body on the island in the bay. Authorities were unsure of her identity, and police dubbed her "Baby Grace." Police distributed composite sketches of the girl nationwide, and Sheryl Sawyers, the girl's paternal grandmother, contacted police from her Ohio home to say the drawing resembled her granddaughter. DNA testing confirmed the child's identity. According to an affidavit, Trenor told police Riley had been beaten and thrown across a room and that her head was held underwater before she died on July 24, 2007. She said the couple hid the girl's body in a storage shed for one to two months before they put it in the plastic container and dumped it into the bay. A medical examiner said Riley's skull was fractured in three places, injuries that would have been fatal. A cross has since been erected on the island where the child was found, which was named Riley's Island in her honor, the Houston Chronicle reported. Trenor moved to Texas from Ohio with the girl in May 2007 to be with Zeigler, whom Trenor had met on the Internet. While in custody, Trenor gave birth this summer to another child, who is now in the care of relatives, Stickler said.

Kimberly Dawn Trenor, 20, is scheduled to stand trial next week in the death of her daughter. She has pleaded not guilty to the capital murder charge, her attorney said Wednesday.

Trenor and her husband, Royce Clyde Zeigler II, 25, were both charged with tampering with evidence and capital murder in the death of Riley Ann Sawyer. The child’s body was discovered in a large blue plastic container on an uninhabited island in Galveston Bay in October 2007. The evidence-tampering charge accused the couple of concealing the child’s remains.

Trenor was arraigned Tuesday in Galveston, according to her attorney, Tom Stickler. Jury selection in her capital murder trial begins Wednesday, and the trial is scheduled to begin in earnest on January 27, he said.

The jury will also sentence Trenor on the evidence-tampering charge, which carries a prison term of two to 20 years, The Houston Chronicle reported.

Zeigler, who will be tried separately, has not yet been formally arraigned, Stickler said. Both remain in jail. Bail was set at $850,000 each, according to the Chronicle.

Riley Ann’s case drew national attention after a fisherman discovered her body on the island. Because authorities initially could not identify her, police called her “Baby Grace.”

Police distributed composite sketches of the child nationwide. Sheryl Sawyers, Riley’s paternal grandmother, contacted police from her home in Ohio after noticing that the drawing resembled her granddaughter. DNA testing later confirmed the child’s identity.

According to an affidavit, Trenor told police that Riley had been beaten and thrown across a room and that her head had been held underwater before she died on July 24, 2007. Trenor said the couple concealed the child’s body in a storage shed for one to two months before placing it in the plastic container and dumping it in the bay.

A medical examiner said Riley’s skull had been fractured in three places and that the injuries would have been fatal.

A cross has since been erected on the island where the child was found, and the site was named Riley’s Island in her honor, the Chronicle reported.

Trenor moved from Ohio to Texas with Riley in May 2007 to be with Zeigler, whom she had met online.

While in custody, Trenor gave birth to another child during the summer. That child is now in the care of relatives, Stickler said.

counterfactuals.output:
## Mother Pleads Guilty to Evidence Tampering in ‘Baby Grace’ Case

**GALVESTON, Texas** — Kimberly Dawn Trenor, the mother of the 2-year-old girl once known publicly as “Baby Grace,” has pleaded guilty to tampering with evidence while awaiting trial on a capital murder charge.

The evidence charge stems from the concealment and disposal of the body of Trenor’s daughter, Riley Ann Sawyers. Investigators said the child’s remains were kept in a plastic container before being dumped in Galveston Bay, where they were discovered by a fisherman in October 2007.

For weeks, authorities were unable to identify the girl and released a forensic sketch under the name “Baby Grace.” Riley was later identified after her paternal grandmother contacted investigators.

Prosecutors allege Trenor and her husband, Royce Clyde Zeigler II, fatally beat the toddler at their home in Spring, Texas, in July 2007. Both were charged with capital murder.

The guilty plea concerns only the handling of Riley’s body and does not resolve the murder charge against Trenor. Sentencing on the tampering conviction was expected to be addressed separately as the capital murder case moved forward.

Attorneys in the murder proceedings have disputed aspects of who was responsible for the child’s death. Both defendants were being prosecuted separately.

# Mother Admits Concealing 2-Year-Old Daughter’s Remains, Pleads Not Guilty to Capital Murder

**GALVESTON, Texas** — Kimberly Dawn Trenor admitted that she helped conceal the remains of her 2-year-old daughter, Riley Ann Sawyers, but pleaded not guilty to a capital murder charge in the child’s death, according to court reports.

Trenor entered the not-guilty plea while acknowledging her role in tampering with evidence by helping place Riley’s body in a container and leaving it near Galveston Bay. The child’s remains were discovered in October 2007 on a small island in the bay, prompting a nationwide effort to identify the girl, initially known publicly as “Baby Grace.”

Authorities allege that Riley died months earlier after suffering prolonged abuse at the suburban Houston home Trenor shared with her husband, Royce Zeigler. Investigators said the child was beaten and thrown onto a hard floor during a disciplinary episode. Her body was then allegedly stored for a period before being placed in a plastic storage container and dumped in the bay.

Trenor’s defense has sought to distinguish her admitted role in concealing the body from responsibility for the killing itself. Her plea means prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that she was legally responsible for Riley’s death, not merely that she participated in efforts to hide it.

Zeigler was also charged with capital murder. Each defendant has blamed the other for the fatal violence, according to accounts of statements given to investigators.

The case drew widespread attention after a fisherman found the container holding Riley’s remains. Because police initially did not know the child’s identity, investigators released forensic sketches and descriptions of clothing and other items found with her. The girl was eventually identified after relatives saw the images and contacted authorities.

Riley had moved to Texas with her mother after Trenor began a relationship with Zeigler. Investigators said the abuse occurred at the couple’s home in Spring, north of Houston.

Under Texas law, a capital murder conviction can carry the death penalty or life imprisonment without parole. Prosecutors’ sentencing options depend on whether they elect to seek death.

The admission concerning concealment could still expose Trenor to punishment on a tampering charge, but it does not amount to a guilty plea to murder. The central issue for jurors would be whether Trenor participated in, intended or was otherwise criminally responsible for the acts that caused her daughter’s death.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened in the Galveston Bay “Baby Grace” case, and what are the current legal proceedings involving Kimberly Dawn Trenor and Royce Clyde Zeigler II?
counterfactuals.output:
### What happened

“Baby Grace” was the name initially given to an unidentified toddler whose body was found in October 2007 inside a plastic storage container in Galveston Bay, Texas. She was later identified as **two-year-old Riley Ann Sawyers**.

Investigators determined that Riley had been killed in July 2007 at the Spring, Texas, home of her mother, **Kimberly Dawn Trenor**, and her stepfather, **Royce Clyde Zeigler II**. Evidence and Trenor’s statements described prolonged physical abuse, including beatings with belts, having Riley’s head held under water, and being thrown onto a tile floor, causing fatal head injuries. The couple concealed her body for weeks and then dumped the container in the bay.

### Criminal cases

- **Kimberly Dawn Trenor** was convicted of capital murder in 2009. Because prosecutors did not seek the death penalty, she received the mandatory sentence of **life imprisonment without parole**.
- **Royce Clyde Zeigler II** was separately convicted of capital murder later in 2009 and likewise sentenced to **life without parole**.

Both challenged their convictions through the appellate process, but the convictions were affirmed.

### Present legal status

The original prosecutions and ordinary direct appeals have concluded. Both convictions remain in effect, and both Trenor and Zeigler remain under Texas life-without-parole sentences. There is no publicly reported pending retrial, resentencing, parole proceeding, or scheduled release for either defendant.

They can still attempt collateral challenges—such as state or federal habeas-corpus petitions—but those proceedings do not undo the convictions unless a court grants relief. Live docket information should be checked through the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals, the relevant federal district court, or Galveston County records for any newly filed petition.
